docs.title: Кодекс Разумного Созидания / Codex of Rational Creation
docs.text:
Добро пожаловать в проект, посвященный деятельной человеческой этике, правде и созидательному развитию.

Welcome to the project dedicated to active human ethics, truth, and constructive development.

docs.title: 🇷🇺 На русском языке
docs.text:
Этот проект — попытка собрать воедино принципы, которые помогут обществу договариваться и созидать в эпоху перемен.

  • Читать Кодекс — основное ядро и принципы.
  • Инструменты — чеклисты для медиа, переговоров и принятия решений.
  • Скачать PDF — версии для печати и чтения офлайн.

docs.title: 🇺🇸 In English
docs.text:
This project is an attempt to bring together principles that help society agree and create in an era of change.

  • Read the Codex — the core principles and foundations.
  • Tools — checklists for media, negotiations, and decision-making.
  • Download PDF — versions for printing and offline reading.

docs.title: О проекте / About
docs.text:
Кодекс не является идеологией или религией. Это рабочий этический стандарт для тех, кто принимает решения и несет ответственность за последствия.

The Code is not an ideology or a religion. It is a working ethical standard for those who make decisions and bear responsibility for the consequences.

GitHub Repository: dkuthering-lab/book-of-blueprint

docs.title: Новая логика структуры
docs.text:
Чтобы Кодекс был "рабочим и принятым", материалы разделены на два слоя:

  • ru/KODEKS/PRINYATYY_KODEKS — действующее ядро (что принимаем как норматив).
  • ru/KODEKS/KONTEKST_EPOKHI — внешние условия, гипотезы, спорные и аналитические блоки.

KODEKS — это один Кодекс. Не отдельные параллельные книги.

docs.title: 1) Рекомендуемый: Docker-образ
docs.text:
По умолчанию используется:

  • card-book-pandoc:latest

Можно указать другой образ:

PANDOC_IMAGE=my-pandoc-image:tag ./scripts/export_pdf.sh

Настройка шрифтов (актуально для кириллицы):

MAIN_FONT="Noto Serif" SANS_FONT="Noto Sans" MONO_FONT="Fira Mono" ./scripts/export_pdf.sh

Настройка формата страницы и полей:

GEOMETRY="a5paper,top=16mm,bottom=18mm,inner=16mm,outer=14mm" ./scripts/export_pdf.sh

По умолчанию скрипт уже собирает в формате A5 с умеренно узкими полями. Главы начинаются с новой страницы (режим book + chapter division). Дополнительно подключается стиль books/EDITIONS/pdf-style.tex для переносов и аккуратного набора.

Изображения на титульных страницах (верхний левый угол) подставляются автоматически. Можно переопределить через переменные окружения:

COVER_KODEKS="source/a_kodex.png" \
COVER_KODEKS_EN="source/a_kodex.png" \
COVER_ALL="source/0_common.png" \
COVER_OBSHCHEE_BLAGO="source/f_patent.png" \
COVER_TEKHNOKOSMOS="source/0_common.png" \
COVER_KARKAS_SMYSLOV="source/b_zapovedi.png" \
./scripts/export_pdf.sh

Подгонка размера/отступа изображения:

COVER_WIDTH="55mm" COVER_X="2mm" COVER_Y="2mm" COVER_PAGES="1" ./scripts/export_pdf.sh

Базовый словарь для консистентного перевода ключевых понятий проекта.

  • созидание -> constructive action

docs.title: Task of the Volume
docs.text: To show that reverence is possible without mystification: through honest knowledge of the world. Man is not the center of the universe, but neither is he dust without meaning. He is a carrier of consciousness capable of understanding and preserving the complexity of the world.

docs.title: Cosmogenesis: We are Part of a Large History
docs.text:
The universe has existed for about 13.8 billion years. Earth — about 4.5 billion. Man as a biological species — about 300 thousand years. Written history — about 5 thousand years.

This is not a reason for nihilism. It is a reason for precision: we are late participants in a very long process of matter's complexification. Our ability to understand this process is in itself a rare and valuable phenomenon.

Practical conclusion: decisions that destroy complexity (ecosystems, cultures, institutions, knowledge) are a step backward on the scale that the Universe has been building for billions of years.

docs.title: Biogenesis: Life as Complexification
docs.text:
Life is not random noise, but a stable reproduction of complexity. Every living organism is a system that resists entropy, accumulates information, and passes it on to the next generations.

Man inherited this ability and expanded it: we pass on not only genes, but also knowledge, culture, institutions, language.

Practical conclusion: to destroy the living means to destroy what was built over millions of years. This requires a very strong justification.

docs.title: Noogenesis: Language, Culture, Science
docs.text:
The emergence of language, writing, science, and technology is not a break from nature, but its continuation. Man became the first being capable of modeling the future, testing hypotheses, and passing on accumulated knowledge through generations without biological evolution.

This expands responsibility: we can foresee the consequences of our actions for decades ahead. This means we are obliged to do so.

docs.title: Working Thought of the Volume
docs.text: Knowledge about the origin of the world and man does not diminish meaning — it deepens it. Constructive action in the logic of the Code is a continuation of what the Universe has been doing for billions of years: complexification, not simplification; order, not chaos; transmission, not destruction.

docs.title: Task of the Volume
docs.text: To show how the values of the Code translate into specific actions. Not an accusatory, but an active tone: fewer slogans, more clear steps.

docs.title: 1. Counteracting Entropy
docs.text:
Everything complex requires effort to maintain. Relationships, knowledge, institutions, health — without attention, they degrade.

Simple actions: - regularly check that important things are not neglected; - notice early signs of destruction before they become a crisis; - invest effort in maintenance, not just in creating something new.

Typical mistake: thinking that "it holds itself" until it breaks. Criterion of progress: important things in life become more stable, not more fragile.

docs.title: 2. Returning Resource to the Cycle
docs.text:
Constructive action is not only the creation of the new, but also the return of what has been received: knowledge, help, time, attention.

Simple actions: - share what you have learned with those who need it; - help not only when it is convenient; - do not accumulate resources beyond reasonable need.

Typical mistake: taking from the common without returning anything back. Criterion of progress: people around you receive more from you than you take.

docs.title: 3. Sufficiency instead of Excessive Consumption
docs.text:
Sufficiency is not asceticism. It is a conscious choice not to take more than is needed for the task and a dignified life.

Simple actions: - before a purchase or decision, ask: "is this needed or just wanted"; - notice when "more" stops giving "better"; - free up space (physical, temporal, attention) for what is important.

Typical mistake: confusing prosperity with accumulation for the sake of accumulation. Criterion of progress: life becomes clearer, not heavier, from the number of things and obligations.

docs.title: 4. Expanding the Horizon through Learning and Practice
docs.text:
A person who has stopped learning begins to shrink. Learning is not only school and books, but any experience reflected upon honestly.

Simple actions: - regularly read or listen to what expands the understanding of the world; - analyze your mistakes without self-flagellation — as a source of data; - try something new long enough to understand if it works.

Typical mistake: thinking that you already know everything in your field. Criterion of progress: in a year you understand something important that you did not understand before.

docs.title: General Criterion of the Way
docs.text: The Way in the logic of the Code is not reaching a final point, but a steady movement towards greater complexity, responsibility, and understanding. If life becomes clearer, relationships — more honest, and decisions — more far-sighted, the Way is working.

docs.title: Why this Volume
docs.text: Rules without examples quickly become dead. Human stories of choice, price, and responsibility are needed. Biographical case studies in the Code are not icons for worship, but working models: how a specific person in specific circumstances made a choice in favor of constructive action.

docs.title: Format of an Article
docs.text:
Each biographical case study is built according to a single scheme:

  1. Brief biography — who this person is, in what context they acted.
  2. Two key episodes — specific situations of choice where the principles of the Code manifested in action.
  3. 3–5 applicable lessons — what from this experience can be transferred to one's own life.
  4. Practice of memory — a specific action that helps to retain the lesson.

docs.title: Pioneers
docs.text: People who opened new paths — in science, technology, social life — and at the same time maintained responsibility to those who will come after. Example type: a scientist who published data openly, knowing that it would slow down his career but accelerate overall progress.

docs.title: Guardians of Order
docs.text: People who held institutions, rules, and agreements at a time when it was more profitable to break them. Example type: a judge, official, or military officer who refused to carry out an illegal order and accepted the price for it.

docs.title: Ascetics of Progress
docs.text: People who consciously chose sufficiency — giving up the excessive for the sake of the quality of work and life. Example type: an entrepreneur or scientist who could have earned more but chose a smaller scale for the sake of greater honesty.

docs.title: Researchers of Harmony
docs.text: People who sought a balance between contradictory values — and found it not in compromise, but in a deeper understanding. Example type: a diplomat or public figure who found a solution where others saw only conflict.

docs.title: Martyrs of Errors
docs.text: People who publicly admitted their mistakes, corrected them, and continued their work — without breaking down or going into denial. Example type: a scientist or journalist who published a refutation of their own work when new data appeared.

docs.title: Conductors of Consciousness
docs.text: Media creators, writers, artists who used their influence to increase the quality of thinking, rather than for manipulation. Example type: an author who refused a lucrative contract because the material would have been harmful to the audience.

docs.title: Sowers (Educators and Teachers)
docs.text: Teachers, mentors, parents who passed on not only knowledge, but also a culture of honest thinking and responsible action. Example type: an educator who created an environment where a mistake is part of learning, not a reason for shame.

docs.title: Public Witnesses (Journalists)
docs.text: Journalists and reporters who documented reality honestly — even when it was dangerous or unprofitable. Example type: a reporter who gave up a sensation for the sake of accuracy and lost in reach, but maintained the audience's trust.

docs.title: Principle of Selecting Case Studies
docs.text:
A biographical case study is included in the Code if:

  • the person's choice was real (there was an alternative, there was a price);
  • the example is applicable to modern situations;
  • the story does not idealize the person, but shows a specific choice in specific circumstances.

Examples from different cultures, eras, and professions are intentional: constructive action does not have one nationality or one profession.

docs.title: Idea
docs.text: Meaning is maintained by repetition. Regular practice here is not about mysticism, but about action that changes the quality of life.

docs.title: Section Framework
docs.text:
• morning rule;
  • weekly practice of service;
  • reviewing mistakes without shame;
  • practice of sufficiency;
  • practices of memory and continuity.

docs.title: Quality Principle
docs.text: A practice is considered good if, after it, order, respect for people, and clarity of thought have increased in life.

docs.title: Supporting Thought
docs.text: The Code does not replace faith and does not fight it. It sets the ethics of action in a common earthly home — a space that people with different beliefs are forced to share.

docs.title: Where the Code and Religion Coincide
docs.text:
Most religious traditions share the key values of the Code:

  • human dignity as the basis of relationships;
  • responsibility for the consequences of one's actions;
  • care for the weak and vulnerable;
  • honesty as a norm, not an exception;
  • respect for labor and constructive action.

Where these values coincide, the Code and the religious tradition strengthen each other, rather than compete.

docs.title: Where the Boundary Lies
docs.text:
Personal faith is a person's internal affair. The Code does not interfere in theology, rites, prayer, and spiritual practice.

The boundary begins where religious norms claim compulsory application in the common public space — especially if this leads to discrimination, humiliation, or violence against other people.

Principle: freedom of faith — yes. Compulsion to faith or punishment for its absence — no.

docs.title: How to Read the Code Alongside Religious Texts
docs.text:
The Code does not replace sacred texts and does not claim their authority. It works on a different level: not "what is true in eternity," but "how we can agree on living together here and now."

A believer can accept the Code as a practical framework for social behavior without giving up their faith. A secular person can accept it without religious justification. This is the meaning of the neutral language of the Code.

docs.title: How to Avoid Alienation
docs.text:
• Do not use the language of the Code as a weapon against believers ("you are backward").
  • Do not use religious language as a weapon against the Code ("this is godlessness").
  • Seek a common language through specific consequences: what improves people's lives, what destroys them.
  • Recognize that different traditions have accumulated real experience of care, community life, and ethics — this experience is valuable.

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: The Code is compatible with faith where faith serves human dignity and the common good. It comes into conflict with faith where it requires humiliation, compulsion, or closing the common space for others.

docs.title: Media Creators as Conductors of Meaning
Why this is Part of the Code
docs.text:
Technology without language and images does not become culture. A media creator is a person who shapes how other people understand the world, make decisions, and relate to each other.

This makes the work of a media creator socially significant — regardless of the size of the audience. A blogger with a thousand followers and an editor of a major publication bear the same ethical responsibility for the consequences of their materials.

docs.title: Criterion for a Media Creator's Work in the Logic of the Code
docs.text:
Not reach and not hype, but contribution to understanding, maturity, and respect for the truth.

Good work of a media creator after publication: - increases clarity for the audience; - helps people act more reasonably; - strengthens trust, rather than destroying it.

Bad work: - exploits fear, anger, or humiliation for the sake of engagement; - replaces facts with a convenient interpretation; - normalizes cynicism and irresponsibility.

docs.title: Types of Media Creators in the Code
Educator-Engineer
docs.text: Translates complex knowledge into understandable language without losing precision. Their task is not to simplify beyond recognition, but to make it accessible without distortion.

docs.title: Psychological Guide
docs.text: Helps the audience understand their own reactions, fears, and motives. Works with vulnerability carefully, rather than exploiting it.

docs.title: Culture Weaver
docs.text: Creates images, stories, and formats that strengthen common values and help people see themselves as part of something larger.

docs.title: Philosopher of Order
docs.text: Asks questions that are uncomfortable but necessary. Not for provocation, but for clarification.

docs.title: Curator of Errors
docs.text: Honestly analyzes failures — their own and others' — as a source of knowledge, rather than as a reason for bullying or self-flagellation.

docs.title: Journalist as a Public Witness
docs.text: Documents reality honestly, even when it is unprofitable or dangerous. Their job is to make visible what power or the market would prefer to hide.

docs.title: Practical Standards
docs.text:
A media creator in the logic of the Code:

  • checks facts before publication;
  • distinguishes between fact, interpretation, and opinion;
  • does not use emotional manipulation as a primary tool;
  • thinks about the consequences of publication for specific people;
  • is ready to publicly correct an error.

docs.title: Central Idea
docs.text:
Education is not a "service" or a "utility." It is the work of shaping a human being: their ability to think, act responsibly, and respect others.

In the world of the Code, educators and teachers are part of the core of creators — on par with scientists, engineers, and doctors. Their labor determines the quality of the next generation of decisions.

docs.title: What it Means to be an Educator in the Logic of the Code
docs.text:
An educator in the logic of the Code:

  • teaches how to think, not just how to memorize;
  • creates an environment where a mistake is part of learning, not a reason for shame or punishment;
  • passes on not only knowledge, but also a culture of checking, updating, and honestly revising knowledge;
  • respects the dignity of each student regardless of their success;
  • remains a student themselves — updates their methods and views when new data appears.

docs.title: New Status Framework
docs.text:
An educator is not "service personnel" of the education system. It is a person who shapes the society's capacity for constructive action.

A society that does not respect educators undermines its own future. The Code considers pedagogical labor as strategically important — no less important than defense or the economy.

docs.title: Morning Circle
docs.text: A short joint practice at the beginning of the day: what is important today, what we want to do well. It forms the habit of a conscious start, rather than a reactive movement according to the schedule.

docs.title: Evening Reflection
docs.text: Review of the day: what worked, what didn't, what can be done differently. Without self-flagellation — as data analysis, not as a trial.

docs.title: Reviewing Mistakes without Shame
docs.text: An error is analyzed publicly as a teaching case: what happened, why, what could have been done differently. This forms a culture of honesty and reduces the fear of failure.

docs.title: Practice of Continuity
docs.text: Older students pass on experience to younger ones. This strengthens both: some learn to explain, others — to receive knowledge from peers.

docs.title: Updating Teacher Training
docs.text:
An educator who does not update their methods gradually teaches the past, not the present.

The Code assumes that the pedagogical community:

  • Regularly exchanges living practices (assemblies, open lessons, reviews);
  • Honestly evaluates what works and what doesn't;
  • Does not hold on to methods out of habit, but changes them when better ones appear.

docs.title: Biographical Case Studies
docs.text: Educators who changed the culture of thinking of their students — not through coercion, but through creating an environment where thinking was interesting and safe. Their examples are analyzed in Volume 3 (Biographical Case Studies).

docs.title: Main Thought
docs.text: Relationships with close people are not a "private trifle," but a basic form of constructive action. Through them, a person learns truth, responsibility, patience, and respect for another's vulnerability.

docs.title: What is Considered Constructive Action in Closeness
docs.text:
• regular live communication, not formal contact;
  • practical help, especially when a person is in difficulty;
  • honest conversation about pain and boundaries without humiliation;
  • readiness to change one's behavior, rather than just demanding changes from another.

docs.title: Mistakes as Signals
docs.text: Conflict does not always mean "everything is broken." Often it is a signal for reassembling the relationship: to clarify expectations, to apologize, to make a new agreement.

docs.title: When Separation Can Be Ethical
docs.text:
If a relationship consistently reproduces lies, humiliation, or the destruction of personality, then an honest separation can be more constructive than prolonged destructive action.

Principle: do not take revenge and do not nullify the past, but complete it carefully, with recognition of the value of the lived experience.

docs.title: Consciousness of Choice
docs.text:
Closeness is a choice that is confirmed by actions. Without choosing consciously, a person often slides into automatism, resentment, and mutual exhaustion.

Therefore, in the Code, maturity is checked not only by social projects, but also by how a person behaves with those who are nearby every day.

docs.title: Journalism as Service to Truth and Society
Why this is Important Labor
docs.text: Journalism makes visible the lives of people, real achievements, and systemic problems. Without this work, society loses feedback and the ability to correct mistakes.

docs.title: Creative Role of Journalism
docs.text:
• show what works in society and gives results;
  • identify problems before they become a catastrophe;
  • give a voice to those who are usually not heard;
  • connect facts, context, and human consequences.

docs.title: Ethical Standard in the Code
docs.text:
A journalist in the logic of the Code:

  • checks facts before publication;
  • separates fact, interpretation, and opinion;
  • does not trade in fear, hatred, and humiliation;
  • remembers that every material has social consequences.

docs.title: What is Considered Destruction
docs.text:
• clickbait, manipulation, and fabrication;
  • replacing investigation with bullying;
  • choosing an agenda only on the principle of profitable noise;
  • normalization of cynicism, when a lie is justified by profit.

docs.title: Practical Criterion
docs.text:
Good journalism after publication increases clarity, responsibility, and the possibility of action. Bad journalism increases panic, aggression, and powerlessness.

docs.title: Biographical Case Studies: Two Applied Examples
1) Investigative Journalist: Anna Politkovskaya
docs.text:
Situation: Worked in the field, documented war crimes, torture, corruption, and abuse of power where silence was more profitable for many. Choice: Put the verified fact above personal safety and career comfort. Price: Constant threats, pressure, eventually murder.

Lessons for the Code:

  • truth requires courage and the discipline of verification;
  • investigation is a service to society, not a personal war;
  • the price of public lies is often measured in human lives;
  • protecting journalists is part of protecting the public good.

Practice of Memory: Once a year, hold an open editorial session "Complex Truth": analyze one material where publication really protected people.

docs.title: 2) Local Journalist as an Agent of Change: "City Editorial" Format
docs.text:
Situation: A small city editorial office systematically covers everyday problems: dilapidated schools, accessibility of the environment, water quality, corruption in procurement. Choice: Do not chase national hype, but conduct long-term work locally. Result: After a series of publications, inspections are launched, facilities are repaired, public reports and new control rules appear.

Lessons for the Code:

  • journalism begins with the visibility of what is nearby, not just "big topics";
  • steady attention to a problem is often more effective than a one-time sensation;
  • the success of journalism is not only reach, but specific improvements in people's lives;
  • a local editorial office can be a pillar of civic trust.

Practice of Memory: Keep a "log of changes" in the editorial office: record what real decisions were made after publications and what has not yet been brought to a result.

docs.title: Red Flags of Manipulative Material
docs.text: A practical checklist for the reader, editor, and teacher.

docs.title: 5 signs that a material may be manipulative
docs.text:
1. Emotion instead of facts The text pushes for fear, anger, or humiliation, but does not provide verifiable data and sources.

  2. Mixing fact and opinion Evaluations and assumptions are presented as established truth without clear marking.

  3. Convenient culprit A complex problem is reduced to one "enemy," while context and systemic causes are ignored.

  4. Clickbait and artificial urgency The headline promises more than is in the text, and pushes for reactive action "right now."

  5. Opacity of information origin There are no links to primary sources, it is unknown who the author is, how the statements were checked, and where the boundaries of reliability are.

docs.title: How to act if you see 2+ flags
docs.text:
• suspend the emotional reaction;
  • find the primary source;
  • check alternative versions;
  • do not spread the material before checking.

docs.title: For the Code
docs.text: The maturity of a reader is not to "believe one's own," but to check information so as not to become a carrier of panic, lies, and enmity.

docs.title: Politics, Defense, and Ethics of the Agreement
Why this Topic is in the Code
docs.text: Politicians and the military affect the lives of millions of people. Therefore, for them, not only competence and strength are especially important, but also a culture of agreement, maintaining peace, and responsibility for the long-term consequences of decisions.

docs.title: Basic Framework
docs.text: The state and the Code should not come into conflict. The Code strengthens statehood where there is service to citizens, safety, and development of the quality of life.

docs.title: Three Principles for Politicians and the Military
docs.text:
1. Negotiability instead of escalation Strength is needed, but its main function is to prevent destruction, not to produce it.

  2. Creative Patriotism Love for the country is expressed in the quality of institutions, care for people, and respect for the truth, rather than in the cult of enmity.

  3. Double Identity: Nation + Humanity A person can be deeply nationally rooted and at the same time understand the common destiny of the planet.

docs.title: Non-contradiction with the State
docs.text:
The Code proceeds from the fact that:

  • the state is necessary as a system of coordination, safety, and law;
  • criticism of the authorities is permissible as a form of improvement, not undermining the country;
  • loyalty to society is higher than loyalty to the personal interests of groups.

docs.title: Where the Red Line Lies
docs.text:
• it is unacceptable to justify the destruction of peaceful life with "higher goals";
  • it is unacceptable to build identity only on the humiliation of other nations;
  • it is unacceptable to use safety as a cover for lies and corruption.

docs.title: Practical Criterion
docs.text:
A political or military decision is considered creative if it:

  • reduces the probability of long-term destruction;
  • strengthens trust within society;
  • preserves the dignity of its people and does not dehumanize others;
  • improves the sustainability of the country without breaking with humanity.

Related applied tool: books/en/CODEX_CHELOVEKA/12_pyat_printsipov_peregovorov_v_logike_kodeksa.en.md

docs.title: Five Principles of Negotiations in the Logic of the Code
docs.text: A practical guide for politicians, the military, managers, and public leaders.

docs.title: 1. Common Framework of Safety and Dignity
docs.text: First, a minimum common contour is fixed: the protection of life, civil infrastructure, and human dignity cannot be a subject of bargaining.

docs.title: 2. Facts Ahead of Slogans
docs.text: Negotiations are built on verifiable data, not on rhetoric. Each side undertakes to separate fact, evaluation, and requirements.

docs.title: 3. Separation of Conflict Levels
docs.text:
It is necessary to separate:

  • fundamental values;
  • specific interests;
  • technical parameters of execution.

Often a dispute over values is not resolved immediately, but technical de-escalation is already possible.

docs.title: 4. Step-by-step Reciprocity
docs.text:
Negotiability is confirmed by small executable steps with verification, rather than just large declarations.

Formula: "small action -> independent verification -> next action."

docs.title: 5. Horizon after Conflict
docs.text: Each decision is checked by the question: "How will people live with this in 5-10 years?" If a decision sows long-term humiliation and revenge, it is strategically weak, even if tactically advantageous.

docs.title: Quick Test before Signing
docs.text:
• does the agreement reduce the probability of a new escalation;
  • does it preserve the face and dignity of the parties;
  • are the mechanisms for monitoring execution clear;
  • is there space for joint constructive action after the crisis.

docs.title: Five Signs that a Material no longer Serves the Truth
docs.text: A checklist for the author, editor, and producer before publication.

docs.title: 1. I know in advance "whom to blame"
docs.text: If the outcome of the text is determined before checking the facts, it is not an investigation, but a confirmation of one's own position.

docs.title: 2. I am amplifying emotion, not understanding
docs.text: The material is made for the sake of shock, anger, or fear, rather than for the sake of clarity and the ability of people to act reasonably.

docs.title: 3. I am hiding the weak points of my version
docs.text: Data limitations, alternative explanations, and controversial zones are not shown. This destroys trust even with partially correct information.

docs.title: 4. I am replacing public utility with personal traffic
docs.text: Decisions are made according to the reach metric at any cost: headline, editing, formulations push for reactive distribution.

docs.title: 5. I am not thinking about the consequences of publication
docs.text: If the author does not ask the question "what will happen to people after the material is released," they pass the responsibility to algorithms and the crowd.

docs.title: Mini-protocol of Self-check
docs.text:
Before publication, answer in writing:

  • what in the material is confirmed, and what is a hypothesis;
  • whom the text really helps;
  • what is the risk of harm and how it is reduced;
  • what needs to be corrected if part of the conclusions turns out to be incorrect.

If there is no honest answer to two points, the publication is better to be revised.

docs.title: Why this is Part of the Code
docs.text:
Links to sources are not a formality. It is a structure of trust that connects individual statements into a verifiable system of knowledge.

Without sources, knowledge falls apart into fragments and turns into an opinion that cannot be honestly checked.

docs.title: Basic Principle
docs.text:
Every significant statement must have an origin:

  • where the data is taken from;
  • by whom and how it was obtained;
  • where the boundaries of the applicability of the conclusions are.

docs.title: What the Culture of Citation Gives
docs.text:
• Verifiability: any person can follow the path from the conclusion to the primary source.
  • Continuity: new knowledge is built on the previous one, rather than starting from scratch every time.
  • Responsibility: the author does not hide weak points behind rhetoric.
  • Reduction of manipulation: it is more difficult to replace facts with a convenient interpretation.

docs.title: Why Updating Knowledge is Good
docs.text:
Knowledge changes because the quality of observations, methods, and data grows. Revision of conclusions is not a sign of chaos, but a normal mechanism of development.

In the logic of the Code, a mature author knows how to say: "According to old data, we thought so. According to new data, it is more accurate like this."

docs.title: Practical Minimum for Text, Lecture, Video
docs.text:
1. Indicate key sources explicitly.
  2. Separate facts from interpretations.
  3. Mark outdated data and the date of update.
  4. Admit mistakes and publish corrections.

docs.title: Red Flags
docs.text:
• "everyone already knows" without links;
  • replacing sources with retellings of retellings;
  • ban on clarification and revision;
  • shame for changing position when new facts appear.

docs.title: Maturity Criterion
docs.text: The higher the quality of citation and the transparency of updates, the more stable the common knowledge and the higher the society's ability to make reasonable decisions.

This is the only official Codex of the project.

docs.title: Why this is Important
docs.text: The Codex must be executable and understandable "here and now." The planet's context is changing rapidly, so it is better to keep it separate from the normative core.

docs.title: Preamble
docs.text:
We know how to build rockets, edit genomes, and process billions of data points per second. But the question of "how to live together without destroying what we have created" still remains without a clear answer.

This document is for those who make decisions: in the family, in the editorial office, in business, in politics. It doesn't matter how large the scale is. What matters is that decisions have consequences for other people.

The Code does not claim to be a new ideology or religion. It offers a working ethical standard — a set of verifiable principles that help:

  • distinguish constructive action from destructive action,
  • rely on truth and verifiable facts,
  • make decisions with human dignity in mind,
  • connect personal responsibility with the common good,
  • maintain a long horizon of development, rather than just immediate profit.

The Code is compatible with laws, religions, cultures, and traditions. It does not cancel them — it sets a common language for talking about consequences.

docs.text:
A strong society is not afraid of fact-checking and updating conclusions. Changing a position based on new data is maturity, not weakness.

Good is what strengthens life, trust, and opportunities. Bad is what brings profit at the cost of destroying people, the environment, and the future.

docs.title: 1) Close Relationships as Labor
docs.text:
Constructive action begins not only with large projects, but also with the quality of relationships with loved ones:

  • respect,
  • dialogue,
  • help,
  • responsibility for one's actions.

Relationships with loved ones are not a "private trifle," but a basic form of constructive action: through them, a person learns truth, responsibility, and respect for another's vulnerability.

What this means in practice:

  • regular live communication, not formal contact;
  • practical help, especially when a person is in difficulty;
  • honest conversation about pain and boundaries without humiliation;
  • readiness to change one's behavior, rather than just demanding changes from another.

Conflict does not always mean "everything is broken." Often it is a signal for reassembly: to clarify expectations, to apologize, to make a new agreement. If a relationship consistently reproduces lies or the destruction of personality, an honest separation can be more creative than prolonged destruction.

docs.title: 2) Regular Practices
docs.text:
Values are stable only when they translate into repeatable actions. Meaning is maintained by repetition — not through mysticism, but through action that changes the quality of life.

Examples of practices:

  • Morning rule — a short check: what is important today and why.
  • Fact-checking — do not spread unverified information, clarify the source before sharing.
  • Reviewing mistakes without shame — analyzing what went wrong, without self-flagellation and without shifting blame.
  • Useful team actions — contribution to the common cause, not just personal efficiency.
  • Practice of sufficiency — a conscious choice not to take more than is needed for the task.
  • Practice of memory and continuity — passing on experience, not just accumulating it.

A practice is considered good if, after it, order, respect for people, and clarity of thought have increased in life.

docs.title: VI. Earth and Space: A Common Horizon
docs.text:
Why is this topic in the Code? Because the choice between "protecting the Earth" and "going into space" is a false dilemma. A civilization that does not care for its foundation will not survive long enough to go beyond it. A civilization that does not look beyond the Earth risks concentrating all vulnerabilities in one point.

Earth and space do not compete. Earth is the foundation of life, culture, and responsibility. Space is the horizon for the sustainable expansion of opportunities and the long-term security of humanity.

Any space project must bring measurable benefit to life on Earth and not worsen the basic conditions for people "here and now." Any earthly project must strengthen humanity's capacity for exploration and constructive action, rather than closing this horizon.

docs.title: VII. Working with Knowledge and Updates
docs.text:
Transparency of sources is not an academic formality. It is an ethical norm.

When a person or institution hides what their statement is based on, they deprive others of the opportunity to check and challenge it. This is a form of power over someone else's thinking. The Code considers such power unacceptable.

Therefore, knowledge in the logic of the Code rests on three requirements:

  • the source is transparent — it is clear where the statement is taken from and who stands behind it;
  • the conclusion is reproducible — another person with the same data can arrive at the same result or honestly challenge it;
  • outdated data is updated publicly — revising a position in the light of new facts is not a weakness, but a sign of maturity.

This applies to journalism, science, politics, business, and personal judgments equally.

docs.title: VIII. Social Contract of the Code
docs.text:
The Code is not a declaration of intent. It is an agreement on how to test decisions in practice.

The agreement works on three levels:

Personal level. A person takes responsibility for the consequences of their words and actions — in the family, in the profession, in the public space.

Social level. Institutions — media, schools, courts, business — are evaluated not by declarations, but by whether they strengthen trust and the quality of people's lives.

Civilizational level. Technologies, economic models, and political decisions are tested on a long horizon: what will remain in 20–50 years?

docs.title: Performance Criterion
docs.text:

  • it has become clearer who the decision really helps and who it harms;
  • the probability of long-term destruction has decreased;
  • trust between participants has grown;
  • the decision can be openly explained to any person it affects.

In a broader horizon, the Code works if the following grow in society:

  • quality of life,
  • level of trust,
  • society's ability to learn,
  • sustainability of decisions in the long horizon.

docs.title: Preamble
docs.text:
We know how to build rockets, edit genomes, and process billions of data points per second. But the question of "how to live together without destroying what we have created" still remains without a clear answer.

This document is for those who make decisions: in the family, in the editorial office, in business, in politics. It doesn't matter how large the scale is. What matters is that decisions have consequences for other people.

The Code does not claim to be a new ideology or religion. It offers a working ethical standard — a set of verifiable principles that help:

  • distinguish constructive action from destructive action,
  • rely on truth and verifiable facts,
  • make decisions with human dignity in mind,
  • connect personal responsibility with the common good,
  • maintain a long horizon of development, rather than just immediate profit.

The Code is compatible with laws, religions, cultures, and traditions. It does not cancel them — it sets a common language for talking about consequences.

docs.title: 1) Close Relationships as Labor
docs.text:
Constructive action begins not only with large projects, but also with the quality of relationships with loved ones:

  • respect,
  • dialogue,
  • help,
  • responsibility for one's actions.

Relationships with loved ones are not a "private trifle," but a basic form of constructive action: through them, a person learns truth, responsibility, and respect for another's vulnerability.

Conflict does not always mean "everything is broken." Often it is a signal for reassembly: to clarify expectations, to apologize, to make a new agreement. If a relationship consistently reproduces lies or the destruction of personality, an honest separation can be more creative than prolonged destruction.

docs.title: 2) Regular Practices
docs.text:
Values are stable only when they translate into repeatable actions. Meaning is maintained by repetition — not through mysticism, but through action that changes the quality of life.

Examples of practices:

  • Morning rule — a short check: what is important today and why.
  • Fact-checking — do not spread unverified information, clarify the source before sharing.
  • Reviewing mistakes without shame — analyzing what went wrong, without self-flagellation and without shifting blame.
  • Useful team actions — contribution to the common cause, not just personal efficiency.
  • Practice of sufficiency — a conscious choice not to take more than is needed for the task.
  • Practice of memory and continuity — passing on experience, not just accumulating it.

A practice is considered good if, after it, order, respect for people, and clarity of thought have increased in life.

docs.title: 3) Media Creators and Educators: Conductors of Meaning
docs.text:
Media creators and educators shape how people understand the world, make decisions, and relate to each other. This makes their work socially significant — regardless of the size of the audience.

Principles of Creative Influence: - responsibility for the quality of the audience's thinking; - priority of clarity over engagement; - respect for the dignity and agency of the student/viewer; - a culture of checking and updating knowledge.

A media creator in the logic of the Code:

  • does not produce content for the sake of engagement at any cost;
  • checks facts and indicates sources;
  • distinguishes between opinion and fact;
  • does not use emotional manipulation as a primary tool.

An educator in the logic of the Code:

  • teaches how to think, not just how to memorize;
  • creates an environment where a mistake is part of learning, not a reason for humiliation;
  • passes on not only knowledge, but also a culture of checking and updating knowledge;
  • respects the dignity of each student regardless of their success.

docs.text:
The Codex is a practical framework to:

docs.title: 15 Core Principles
docs.text:
1. Truth is more important than convenient lies.
  2. Human dignity is inviolable.
  3. Freedom is not the right to harm others.
  4. Constructive action is more important than gain at any cost.
  5. Technology is justified only when it improves quality of life.
  6. Bioprogress is acceptable only where humans are not treated as commodities.
  7. Capital is a tool, not the ultimate goal.
  8. Knowledge must remain verifiable and revisable.
  9. Journalists, media creators, and educators are responsible for the quality of public thinking.
  10. Care for close relationships is part of social construction.
  11. Capacity for agreement is stronger than escalation.
  12. National identity strengthens constructive action, not hostility.
  13. Earth and space form one development contour.
  14. Human rights and development are compatible, not opposed.
  15. Faith and secular ethics can coexist in shared public space.

docs.title: How to apply the Codex
docs.text:
Before any major action, ask four questions:

  1. Who is genuinely helped by this?
  2. What harm is possible, and how is it reduced?
  3. Which sources support this decision?
  4. What happens in 5–10 years if this practice scales?

If answers are unclear, the decision should be revised.

docs.title: Analysis of the Current Situation and Challenges of the Epoch
docs.text: This text serves as a link between the normative core of the Code and the reality of the 2020s. The Code is not created in a vacuum — it is a response to specific destructive processes.

docs.title: 1. Crisis of Trust and Devaluation of Truth
docs.text: We live in an era of "post-truth," where emotional manipulation and algorithmic noise displace verifiable facts. This destroys the society's ability to agree and make rational decisions. Connection with the Code: Section VII "Working with Knowledge."

docs.title: 2. Technological Gap
docs.text: The speed of technology development (AI, bioengineering) outpaces the speed of its ethical comprehension. There is a risk of turning a person into a "biological resource" or an object of algorithmic management. Connection with the Code: Section IV "Economy and Technology."

docs.title: 3. Atomization and Crisis of Meanings
docs.text: Traditional institutions are weakening, and new ones are often built on a cult of consumption or short-term engagement. This leads to the loss of a long planning horizon. Connection with the Code: Section II "Close Relationships" and Section VIII "Social Contract."

docs.title: 4. Planetary Fragility
docs.text:
Environmental and geopolitical risks show that the Earth is a single contour. It is impossible to ensure the safety of one group at the expense of destroying the common foundation. Connection with the Code: Section VI "Earth and Space."

This analysis is not final. It is updated as external conditions change, helping the Code to remain a living tool, rather than a frozen dogma.

1. Does the publication increase clarity and help people act, rather than just react?
  2. Is there a context of causes and consequences, rather than just an "information blow"?
  3. Does the headline correspond to the actual content, without clickbait?

docs.title: D. Responsibility after Release
docs.text:
1. Is there an action plan if an error is discovered (correction, note, explanation)?
  2. Is a person responsible for post-publication monitoring of consequences assigned?
  3. Is the team ready to publicly explain the methodology of the material?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• 10-12 "yes" -> material is ready for publication.
  • 7-9 "yes" -> needs revision and re-checking.
  • 0-6 "yes" -> high risk of destructive effect; stop publication.

docs.title: Negotiations: Quick Decision Checklist
docs.text:
Use before starting, during the process, and before signing agreements.

Mark each item: yes / partially / no.

docs.title: A. Safety and Dignity Framework
docs.text:
1. Are non-negotiable foundations fixed: protection of life, civil infrastructure, and human dignity?
  2. Is there an agreed ban on public dehumanization of the parties?

docs.title: B. Facts and Transparency
docs.text:
1. Are disputed points separated into fact, interpretation, and position?
  2. Is key data verifiable and accessible to both parties?

docs.title: C. Agreement Architecture
docs.text:
1. Are the levels separated: values, interests, technical execution?
  2. Is there a sequence of small executable steps with verification?
  3. Is it clear who and how confirms the execution of each step?

docs.title: D. Horizon after Conflict
docs.text:
1. Does the decision reduce the risk of re-escalation in a 5-10 year horizon?
  2. Is there a adjustment mechanism for failures without immediate disruption of the entire process?
  3. Does the agreement create space for joint constructive action after the crisis?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• 8-10 "yes" -> negotiable construction, can proceed to implementation.
  • 5-7 "yes" -> launch only in pilot mode with mandatory revision.
  • 0-4 "yes" -> high probability of failure and intensification of conflict; framework reassembly needed.

docs.title: Framework Status
docs.text: The Code is compatible with universal human rights and cannot be interpreted as a basis for their arbitrary restriction.

docs.title: Basic Pillars of Compatibility
docs.text:
The Code proceeds from the recognition of:

  • the dignity of each person;
  • the inadmissibility of dehumanization and humiliation;
  • the equal value of life and basic safety;
  • freedom of thought, conscience, and peaceful participation in public life;
  • legal responsibility of institutions to citizens.

docs.title: What this means in practice
docs.text:
1. No "higher goal" justifies a systemic violation of human dignity.
  2. Criticism, discussion, and revision of decisions are a normal part of a mature society.
  3. Safety, development, and order are permissible only together with human rights, not instead of them.

docs.title: Boundary of Application
docs.text:
If a specific measure protects the public good but affects rights, it is permissible only if the following conditions are simultaneously met:

  • legality;
  • proportionality;
  • public transparency;
  • control and the possibility of appeal.

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: The Code does not oppose constructive action to human rights. It considers them a necessary condition for the sustainable development of society and humanity.

docs.title: Accepted Code: Reader's Guide
docs.text: A short guide to the main ideas and tools of the Code.

docs.title: How to read
docs.text:
1. Read 3 basic texts (15-20 minutes).
  2. Choose 1-2 checklists for your role (editor, manager, teacher, community member).
  3. Apply to one real decision.

docs.title: Step 1. Basic Texts
docs.text:
1. books/en/OBSHCHEE_BLAGO_I_SPRAVEDLIVAYA_EKONOMIKA/01_eticheskiy_kriteriy_horosho_i_ploho.en.md A simple evaluation framework: does the decision improve the lives of people and society.

  2. books/en/OBSHCHEE_BLAGO_I_SPRAVEDLIVAYA_EKONOMIKA/06_manifest_obshchego_blaga.en.md Short social contract of the Code.

  3. books/en/KODEKS/PRINYATYY_KODEKS/PRAVA_CHELOVEKA_I_SOVMESTIMOST_KODEKSA.en.md Legal minimum: development not against human rights.

docs.title: Step 2. Applied Tools
docs.text:
• For media: books/en/KODEKS/PRINYATYY_KODEKS/MEDIA_EDITORIAL_CHECKLIST.en.md
  • For negotiations: books/en/KODEKS/PRINYATYY_KODEKS/NEGOTIATION_CHECKLIST.en.md
  • For Earth-Space projects: books/en/KODEKS/PRINYATYY_KODEKS/ZEMLYA_KOSMOS_CHECKLIST.en.md
  • For working with facts: books/en/KODEKS/PRINYATYY_KODEKS/SOURCE_NOTE.en.md

docs.title: Step 3. Mini-practice
docs.text:
Take one current situation (work project, publication, controversial decision) and answer:

  • where is the real benefit for people here;
  • where is the risk of harm;
  • what data confirms the decision;
  • what needs to be changed before launch.

If after checking you see that the decision has become clearer and more honest, the Code is working.

docs.title: Source Policy
docs.text: Short rules for all materials of the "Accepted Code".

docs.title: Mandatory Rules
docs.text:
1. Any significant fact or figure must have a source.
  2. Any source must be formatted through books/en/KODEKS/PRINYATYY_KODEKS/SOURCE_NOTE.en.md.
  3. Fact, interpretation, and opinion are marked separately.
  4. When new data appears, the author updates the conclusion, rather than hiding the discrepancy.

docs.title: Update Rule
docs.text:
• If a source is outdated, a "requires revision" note is placed next to the thesis.
  • The revision is recorded openly: "was / became / why changed".

docs.title: Prohibited Practices
docs.text:
• "retelling of a retelling" as the only source;
  • anonymous "experts" without verifiable qualifications;
  • selecting data only for a pre-selected conclusion.

docs.title: Earth and Space: One Development Contour
Normative Formula
docs.text:
The development of civilization has a single contour:

  • Earth - the foundation of life, culture, and responsibility.
  • Space - the horizon for expanding opportunities and long-term sustainability of humanity.

These vectors do not contradict each other and cannot be separated by the "either-or" principle.

docs.title: Principle of Non-contradiction
docs.text:
Any space project must:

  1. not worsen the basic conditions of life on Earth;
  2. bring knowledge, technology, or organizational solutions useful to society;
  3. take into account long-term environmental and social consequences.

Any earthly project must:

  1. strengthen humanity's capacity for exploration and constructive action;
  2. improve the quality of life without environmental degradation;
  3. support a culture of open knowledge and international cooperation.

docs.title: Practical Decision Test
docs.text:
A decision is considered consistent with the Code if it simultaneously:

  • improves the sustainability of life on Earth;
  • does not close the horizon of scientific and space development;
  • reduces conflict between national interests and the common human good.

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: Protecting the Earth and going into space is one task of a mature humanity, not two competing projects.

docs.title: Earth-Space: Quick Decision Checklist
docs.text:
Use before launching a project, program, law, or major agreement.

Mark each item: yes / partially / no.

docs.title: A. Earthly Foundations
docs.text:
1. Does the project not worsen the basic conditions of life on Earth (water, air, health, safety)?
  2. Are environmental risks taken into account, measurable, and have a reduction plan?
  3. Is there a clear social benefit in a 3-5 year horizon?

docs.title: B. Development Horizon
docs.text:
1. Does the project not close the scientific and space horizon, but expand it?
  2. Are the results of the project converted into knowledge available for further development?
  3. Is there a contribution to long-term sustainability (10+ years), rather than just a short-term effect?

docs.title: C. Social and Political Consistency
docs.text:
1. Does the decision reduce conflict between national interests and the common human good?
  2. Is the management mechanism transparent: is it clear who is responsible for errors and adjustments?
  3. Is human dignity not violated and are groups of "expendable material" not created?

docs.title: D. Culture of Evidence
docs.text: 1. Do key conclusions rely on verifiable sources and have a revision plan based on new data?

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• 8-10 "yes" -> decision is consistent with the "Earth-Space" contour.
  • 5-7 "yes" -> launch only as a pilot, with mandatory revision of weak zones.
  • 0-4 "yes" -> decision requires reassembly; launch increases the risk of destruction.

docs.title: Why a Criterion is Needed
docs.text: When society argues about politics, economics, or technology, usually everyone says "this is right." The Code suggests not arguing only with slogans, but checking the consequences.

docs.title: Basic Check
docs.text:
Good is what:

  • strengthens the life and dignity of people;
  • improves the quality of joint life, rather than the profit of a narrow group;
  • leaves behind more order, trust, and opportunities.

Bad is what:

  • is built on lies, humiliation, or exploitation;
  • improves the lives of some at the expense of the degradation of others;
  • leaves society with long-term destruction (conflict, fear, environmental destruction).

docs.title: Three Questions before a Decision
docs.text:
1. Who will be better off, and who will be worse off? If "profit at the top, damage at the bottom," this is a warning signal.

  2. What will happen in 5-10 years? A decision should not look good only in a short horizon.

  3. Can this be openly explained to an ordinary person? If a decision is shameful to explain directly, it most likely has an ethical defect.

docs.title: Psychology, Sociology, Law — in One Contour
docs.text:
• Psychology: people cooperate better when they feel respect and fairness.
  • Sociology: society is stable when the rules are the same for everyone, not just for the weak.
  • Law: an ethically strong decision must be legal, proportional, and verifiable.

docs.title: Short Formula
docs.text: If a decision improves the quality of life without dehumanization and does not destroy the future, it moves towards "good." If it is profitable today but breaks people and institutions tomorrow, it is "bad," even with beautiful packaging.

docs.title: Main Idea
docs.text: Property is needed by a person for life, freedom, and labor. But in the Code, it is not considered "sacred in itself." Its meaning is in responsible use, not in the right to harm others.

docs.title: What this Changes
docs.text:
Ownership is justified if it:

  • does not destroy the common space of life;
  • does not turn basic goods into a tool of blackmail;
  • helps to create, rather than block development.

docs.title: Where the Boundary Lies
docs.text: My house, my business, my tool — this is a zone of autonomy. But air, water, safety, access to basic infrastructure — this is already a common contour, where personal interest is limited by the public good.

docs.title: Practical Principles
docs.text:
1. An unused resource should not rot. If a resource is held without benefit and interferes with others, society has the right to a mechanism for returning it to circulation according to transparent rules.

  2. Profit does not justify harm. If property brings income at the cost of the degradation of the environment and people, this is a violation, not a "successful business."

  3. Responsibility is measurable. The owner is responsible not only for the right to own, but also for the consequences of use.

docs.title: Why this is Important for an Ordinary Person
docs.text: Such an approach reduces cynicism: people see that the rules apply not only to the weak. And this directly affects trust, safety, and readiness to cooperate.

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: Property in the Code is not a cult of ownership, but a form of agreement: you are given a right, you bear responsibility.

docs.title: Capital as a Tool, not a Goal
What is the Problem with the Old Logic
docs.text: When capital turns into an end in itself, society begins to evaluate people by the volume of accumulated wealth, rather than by the quality of their contribution. This encourages a race for numbers and weakens trust.

docs.title: The Code's Approach
docs.text: Capital is not a moral merit in itself. It is a resource that must work for the development of people, infrastructure, knowledge, and sustainability.

docs.title: The "Capital in Service" Principle
docs.text:
Capital is considered creative if it:

  • expands access to a quality life;
  • supports long-term socially useful projects;
  • reduces chaos and injustice, rather than amplifying them.

docs.title: Where the Imbalance is Visible
docs.text:
• there is profit, but the vulnerability of people and the environment is growing;
  • innovation is presented as progress, but in fact it is squeezing rent;
  • social costs are shifted to those who do not receive the benefit.

docs.title: Practical Filter
docs.text:
Before launching a major financial decision, questions are asked:

  1. What real problem for people does this solve?
  2. Who bears the risks and who receives the benefit?
  3. What will remain for society in 5-10 years, besides a financial report?

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: Capital in the logic of the Code is the energy of development. If it does not serve the common good, it loses ethical legitimacy.

docs.title: Main Fork
docs.text: Society needs both motivation for creators and quick access to useful knowledge. If only monopoly is preserved, progress slows down. If authorship is ignored, the motivation to create falls.

docs.title: The Code's Approach
docs.text:
Formula: honor to the author, benefit to humanity.

This means:

  • the author receives recognition and fair remuneration;
  • critically important knowledge is not blocked by rent for decades;
  • public interest has priority where it concerns life, health, and basic safety.

docs.title: Practical Principles
docs.text:
1. Transparency of the Innovation Source It is clear what was created by a private team and what was built on public resources.

  2. Fair Term of Exclusivity The term should protect the developer's labor, but not turn into a mechanism for slowing down development.

  3. Mandatory Access Mechanisms For vital technologies, models of open licensing or regulated accessibility must work.

docs.title: Risk that is Important to Avoid
docs.text: When a patent is used not to protect labor, but to maintain scarcity, society pays a double price: in money and in lost development time.

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: A patent in the Code is a temporary tool for coordinating interests, not an absolute right to block socially important knowledge.

docs.title: Principle of the Boundary
docs.text: Personal freedom is a basic value. But it ends where a person's actions systematically destroy the safety, dignity, and living conditions of others.

docs.title: What this Means in the Logic of the Code
docs.text:
• freedom does not equal the right to harm;
  • the public good does not equal total control;
  • sanctions are needed not for revenge, but to stop harm and restore justice.

docs.title: When Restriction is Permissible
docs.text:
Restriction of a measure is permissible only if the following conditions are simultaneously met:

  1. legality;
  2. proportionality;
  3. public transparency;
  4. possibility of appeal;
  5. limited and clear term.

docs.title: Which Sanctions are Ethically Preferable
docs.text:
• correction of behavior and an obligation to eliminate harm;
  • restriction of access to privileges if public trust is violated;
  • restorative measures for victims.

Less preferable are measures that are only punitive but do not reduce the risk of recurrence.

docs.title: Where the Risk of Abuse Lies
docs.text:
• vague formulations of "threat";
  • selective application of norms;
  • punishing criticism instead of punishing real harm.

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: A mature system does not choose between "complete permissiveness" and "harsh suppression." It holds freedom and responsibility in one legal contour.

docs.title: Why this Manifesto
docs.text: We live in a common world where consequences do not remain local. Therefore, mature ethics begins with a simple recognition: one cannot build personal well-being on the systemic destruction of the common home.

docs.title: Basic Provisions
docs.text:
1. Common good is the criterion for decisions. A good decision improves the quality of life of people without degradation of the environment and dignity.

  2. Constructive action is more important than profit at any cost. Economic success is not a moral argument if it is achieved through harm.

  3. Knowledge must spread. Sources, citation, and open updating of conclusions are a norm of development, not bureaucracy.

  4. Technology is subordinate to humanity. Progress is justified only where it reduces suffering and expands a dignified life.

  5. Freedom does not equal arbitrariness. Personal freedom ends where sustainable damage to others begins.

docs.title: Social Contract of the Code
docs.text:
We recognize:

  • the value of labor and care;
  • the value of an honest public word;
  • the value of an agreement instead of escalation;
  • the value of national identity without enmity towards others;
  • the value of human rights as the basis for sustainable development.

docs.title: What this Means in Everyday Life
docs.text:
• in the family: respect, dialogue, responsibility for words and actions;
  • in work: quality, honesty, refusal of manipulation;
  • in society: participation, checking information, supporting fair rules;
  • in politics: negotiability, transparency, long horizon.

docs.title: Short Formula of the Manifesto
docs.text: Truth instead of a convenient lie. Constructive action instead of destructive action. Dignity instead of dehumanization. Common good instead of narrow profit.

docs.title: Ethics of Cloning and Human Dignity
Why this Chapter
docs.text: Cloning and related biotechnologies cannot be evaluated only on the principle of "can we or can't we." The main question of the Code: does it improve the quality of life of people and preserve human dignity.

docs.title: Basic Ethical Principle
docs.text: Not everything technically possible is ethically permissible. A person cannot become raw material, expendable material, or a commodity, even if it is economically profitable.

docs.title: What can be Considered Socially Useful
docs.text:
• therapeutic biotechnologies for the treatment of serious diseases;
  • restoration of body functions and reduction of suffering;
  • research that undergoes independent ethical expertise and transparent public control;
  • decisions that give long-term benefit to many, rather than profit to a narrow group.

docs.title: Red Lines
docs.text:
• reproductive human cloning as an industry of "custom-made people";
  • selection of people based on profit, status, or market demand;
  • biotechnological practices that amplify humiliation, discrimination, or social stratification;
  • any decisions without voluntary informed consent and without the right to refuse.

docs.title: Criterion of "Good/Bad" in this Topic
docs.text:
Good, if the technology:

  • reduces pain and expands opportunities to live with dignity;
  • does not destroy equal human dignity;
  • does not turn vulnerable people into an object of exploitation;
  • strengthens the common good and trust in society.

Bad, if the technology:

  • commercializes human life as a product;
  • consolidates a new biological elitism;
  • normalizes the idea that a person's value is determined by utility or price.

docs.title: Principle of Constructive Action for the Sake of Quality of Life
docs.text: Bioprogress is justified where it helps people live longer, healthier, and freer lives without destroying the moral framework of society. Constructive action without dignity is no longer development, but a technical form of destructive action.

docs.title: Ethical Test of Technology: 7 Questions
docs.text: This test is needed for a quick assessment of any technology: from AI and bioengineering to cloning models and new forms of automation.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text: For each question, give an answer: "yes," "partially," or "no." If there is at least one confident "no" in questions 1, 2, 3, or 5, the technology should not be scaled until the risk is eliminated.

docs.title: 7 Questions
docs.text:
1. Dignity: Does the technology not turn a person into an object, raw material, or commodity?

  2. Common Good: Does it improve the quality of life not only of a narrow group, but of society as a whole?

  3. Fairness of Access: Does it not create a new form of biological or technological caste system?

  4. Voluntariness: Is there real informed consent and a right to refuse for the person without hidden punishment?

  5. Non-destruction of the Environment: Does the technology not destroy the natural and social living conditions of future generations?

  6. Transparency and Responsibility: Is it clear who makes decisions, who is responsible for errors, and how damage is corrected?

  7. Creative Outcome: Does the technology increase the space of freedom, development, care, and meaningful labor?

docs.title: Interpretation of the Result
docs.text:
• 7 "yes" -> technology can be implemented with regular public audit.
  • 5-6 "yes" + "partially" -> pilot mode, limited scale, mandatory revision.
  • Less than 5 "yes" -> implementation is postponed until ethical failures are eliminated.

docs.title: For the Topic of Human Cloning
docs.text: The test does not block research "by default," but strictly limits practices where human life loses dignity for the sake of profit, status, or market demand.

docs.title: Central Thought
docs.text: A person is not just a consumer of services and goods. He is a participant in common development, on which the quality of life of other people and the future of society depend.

docs.title: Basic Framework
docs.text:
This book offers a practical ethics in which:

  • meaning is born in action, not in declarations;
  • human dignity is more important than profit at any cost;
  • knowledge and constructive action are more important than information noise.

docs.title: Five Supporting Principles
docs.text:
1. Truth and Verifiability Speak and act so that words can be checked.

  2. Constructive Action instead of Exploitation Evaluate decisions by real benefit for people, rather than by short-term profit.

  3. Sufficiency and Responsibility for Resources Consume reasonably, without shifting the environmental and social debt to others.

  4. Growth through Learning and Revision Changing a position based on new data is a sign of maturity.

  5. Solidarity and Respect for Dignity One cannot build "one's success" on the humiliation or dehumanization of others.

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: This framework does not require a single ideology. It requires honesty of thinking, responsibility for consequences, and respect for the person.

docs.title: Why such Spaces are Needed
docs.text:
People need places where they can not only consume content, but also think together, learn, and do useful things.

It is not about religious institutions, but about spaces of social maturation.

docs.title: Types of Spaces
docs.text:
• Workshops of Action Places where people repair, design, teach, and share skills together.

  • Halls for Reviewing Mistakes A format for open analysis of failures without bullying, with the aim of improving practices.

  • Observatories and Science Clubs Places where respect for knowledge and a large-scale view of the world are developed.

  • Centers for Public Dialogue Platforms for negotiations, local solutions, and joint initiatives.

docs.title: Principle of Operation
docs.text:
A good place of power:

  • does not produce a cult of the leader;
  • does not require blind loyalty;
  • measures value through contribution and quality of interaction.

docs.title: Criterion of Usefulness
docs.text: If after participation people become calmer, more accurate in thinking, and more active in creative actions, the space fulfills its function.

docs.title: What is Understood here by Ritual
docs.text: These are regular actions that help to maintain attention, discipline, and respect for each other. They should not be a tool of pressure.

docs.title: Why they are Needed
docs.text: Without repeatable practices, values quickly fall apart into beautiful words. With practices, values turn into stable behavior.

docs.title: Examples of Neutral Practices
docs.text:
• short morning focus: "what I will improve today";
  • weekly review of team mistakes without searching for a "culprit";
  • socially useful action according to the schedule (repair, help, training);
  • personal practice of fact-checking before spreading information.

docs.title: Boundary between Practice and Violence
docs.text:
A practice becomes harmful when:

  • there is no right to refuse or pause;
  • humiliation for "insufficient involvement" is used;
  • form becomes more important than meaning and result.

docs.title: Principle of Voluntariness
docs.text: Participation must be conscious. A strong practice invites, rather than breaks.

docs.title: Why this is Important
docs.text: If society respects only money and consumption status, it encourages cynicism. The Code offers another logic: recognition by the quality of contribution to common development.

docs.title: What is Considered a Contribution
docs.text:
• work that really improves people's lives;
  • honest transmission of knowledge and upbringing of the next generation;
  • creation of solutions that reduce chaos and injustice;
  • actions that strengthen trust and negotiability.

docs.title: What is NOT Considered a Contribution
docs.text:
• profit built on manipulation and exploitation;
  • conspicuous consumption as "proof of value";
  • status without responsibility for consequences.

docs.title: How to Avoid a New Elitism
docs.text:
1. Evaluation criteria must be public.
  2. The possibility of growth must be open to any person.
  3. An error does not exclude from the community if the person recognizes it and corrects it.

docs.title: Short Conclusion
docs.text: A hierarchy by contribution is needed not to divide people into "castes," but for a fair distribution of respect and responsibility.

docs.title: Why this Section
docs.text: Any strong idea can be distorted. To prevent the Code from turning into an ideology of pressure, the risks must be named in advance.

docs.title: Main Risks
docs.text:
1. Cult of the Only Correct Version The space for questions, criticism, and revision disappears.

  2. New Moral Elitism People begin to divide into "pure" and "incorrect" instead of help and development.

  3. Digital Control without Boundaries Metrics and ratings replace living ethics and human dignity.

  4. Replacing Meaning with Procedure The form is observed, but there is no real benefit and honesty.

docs.title: Protection Mechanisms
docs.text:
• the right to reasoned disagreement;
  • independent review of controversial decisions;
  • transparent criteria and public adjustments;
  • mandatory check for compatibility with human rights.

docs.title: Quick Test "Have we gone into Distortion?"
docs.text:
• can current rules be safely criticized;
  • is there a way to correct errors without humiliation;
  • does the system help people become more mature, rather than more dependent.

If there is no confident "yes" to these questions, the framework needs to be revised.

docs.title: Framework of Meanings and Practices
